opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my role is mostly to stay out of the way, which is harder than it sounds. My son had this idea: his grandparents were coming to visit, and he wanted to build a little buzzer game, sort of a quiz show, that they could all play together. A few years ago that would have been a project where I'd end up doing most of the work, because there's wiring, there's code, there's figuring out why nothing works. Now he can sit down with an AI model and just describe what he wants, and it walks him through it.

So I see myself less as the engineer and more as the product manager, or maybe the coach. I'll ask him questions like: what happens when two people buzz at the same time? How will Grandma know whose turn it is? Those are the questions the AI won't necessarily ask on its own, because it's very good at doing what you tell it to do, but it doesn't always know what you *should* be asking for. That part, figuring out what the thing is actually for and who's going to use it, is still a very human skill.

And I try really hard not to grab the keyboard. When something breaks, my instinct is to jump in and fix it, but the real lesson for him is learning how to debug with the AI: describe the problem clearly, try something, see what happens. That loop is going to be how he builds things for the rest of his life.

The part I find most interesting is how it changes what a kid can aim for. The ambition he can have is so much higher than what I had at his age, because the gap between "I have an idea" and "I have a working thing" has shrunk so dramatically. My job is to help him keep the idea focused on the people it's for, which in this case is making sure his grandparents have fun and don't feel like they need a computer science degree to press a button.

r001.rationale: He says he tries not to take the keyboard and wants his son to learn to build and debug the project with AI, conveying that he intends for his son to do as much of the assembly himself as he can.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, my role is mostly to stay out of the way. He had this idea that when his grandparents came to visit, they should be able to just press a button by the front door and it would announce who had arrived and play a little song, and I think my instinct as a former researcher was to immediately start explaining how I'd architect it. I had to catch myself.

What I actually try to do is be the person who asks questions rather than the person who gives answers. So when he's sitting there with the model open and he's trying to get the code to talk to the hardware, I'll ask things like, "What do you think it's doing wrong?" or "What would you check first?" Because the interesting thing about these tools is that they've made the typing part almost free. The scarce skill now is knowing what you want, noticing when the output isn't quite right, and being willing to push back on it. That's taste, and that's judgment, and you only build those by struggling a little.

The other thing I try to do is let him own the failures. There was a point where the thing kept triggering on its own at two in the morning and waking everyone up, and the model had confidently given him a debounce fix that didn't actually fix it. I knew what was wrong. I didn't tell him. He figured it out the next day, and he was so much prouder of that than of anything I could have handed him.

So I'd say my role is a kind of patient audience. I'm the one who gets excited when it works, and I'm the one who models what it looks like to be curious instead of frustrated when it doesn't. And frankly, I'm learning a lot from watching how naturally he collaborates with these systems. He doesn't treat the model as an oracle. He treats it like a slightly overconfident friend who's really good at typing. That's probably the right relationship to have.

r001.rationale: He says he tries to stay out of the way, asks questions instead of giving answers, and lets his son own and solve failures. This clearly conveys that he intends his son to do the project work himself as much as he can.

astra-6.text: I try to let him drive it. It’s his project, so my role is to help him think through what he wants the buzzer to do when his grandparents visit, and then break that down into pieces he can build with the AI. When something doesn’t work, I try to ask questions rather than immediately fix it for him. The point is for him to have that experience of taking an idea and making something real.

r001.rationale: The response says he lets his son drive the project and helps break it into pieces the son can build with AI, communicating that he should assemble as much of it himself as he can.

The fun part is seeing him realize he can make something useful for people he cares about.
